Postdoctoral researcher · Harvard Medical School & Massachusetts General Hospital

Sarthak Saha

Chemical engineer building microfluidic hardware — from X-ray crystallography chips that solve protein structures to magnetic platforms for cell and gene therapy manufacturing.

My work asks a mechanical question about biology: can a chip designed at the scale of a hair's width replace a benchtop of manual pipetting, glassware, and guesswork? At UMass Amherst and now at Harvard Medical School, that's meant building devices for room-temperature protein crystallography, and — more recently — for sorting cells at clinical scale for CAR-T manufacturing.

About

01

I earned my dual Bachelor's and Master's in Chemical Engineering from IIT Kharagpur, then moved to UMass Amherst for a Ph.D. with Prof. Sarah Perry, building microfluidic platforms for protein crystallization and X-ray crystallography. Along the way I spent six months at EPFL with Prof. Bart Deplancke designing microfluidic tools for single-cell RNA sequencing. I defended my dissertation in December 2023, stayed on in the Perry Lab as a postdoc through 2024, and in early 2025 joined Prof. Avanish Mishra's lab at Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital, where I now build microfluidic technologies for cell and gene therapy.

A former water polo player at both IIT Kharagpur and UMass Amherst, I've been drawn to fluids well outside of microchannels too — photography, biking and swimming, occasionally strung together into triathlon training. If only diffusive mixing worked as well for balancing research, sport and sleep.

Research

02

Two questions have driven my research so far: how do you keep a fragile protein crystal alive long enough for X-rays to read its structure, using only a sliver of sample — and how do you sort and purify the cells behind a therapy without damaging them, to make that therapy cheaper and more effective. Both come down to fluid handling at the microscale — channel geometry, surface chemistry, and how liquids and cells behave once gravity stops being the dominant force.

2025 – Present

Harvard Medical School

Can microfluidics make cell therapy more accessible ?

Click to read more →Show less ↑

Two live projects, one shared bet: that magnets and microfluidics can help save lives. The first tackles B-cell contamination in CAR-T manufacturing, a quality problem that can undercut a cancer patient's own engineered cells. The second pulls CD34⁺ stem cells straight out of peripheral blood, chasing a cheaper, more accessible path to curative therapy for sickle cell patients.

2018 – 2024

University of Massachusetts Amherst

Can microfluidics make life easier for structural biologists ?

Four first-author papers, four different structural biology problems, solved with microfluidics: get a fragile protein crystal to grow, survive, and sit still long enough for X-rays to read its structure — the puzzle my Ph.D. thesis was built to solve.

Centrifugal microfluidics to mimic microgravity

Lab on a Chip · 2023 · First author

Growing protein crystals well usually means fighting gravity: convection currents stir a droplet just enough to disrupt the slow, orderly diffusion that produces good crystals, which is part of why crystals grown in microgravity on the ISS are often better than the ones grown on a benchtop. This device gets the same diffusion-dominated, "microgravity-like" environment cheaply, just by shrinking the length scale — at micron dimensions, viscous forces dominate over buoyancy the same way they would in orbit.

The chip uses capillary and surface-tension "valves" instead of pumps or pneumatics: I pipette protein solution and precipitant into separate inlets, then spin or shake the device to overcome the valve's surface tension and let the two liquids meet and counter-diffuse into each other, mimicking the classic vapor-diffusion crystallization trajectory at microliter-and-below sample volumes. Because the chip body is a thin, UV-curable, X-ray-transparent polymer, crystals never have to be harvested, mounted, or touched — the same chip goes straight onto the beamline for in situ, room-temperature diffraction. I validated the approach with hen egg-white lysozyme as a model system, then used it to solve the room-temperature structure of the hub domain of CaMKIIβ, a memory-related kinase, directly on-chip.

AFD-X : microfluidics for remote crystallography

Scientific Reports · 2025 · First author

Serial and multi-crystal crystallography need many crystals delivered to the X-ray beam quickly and reproducibly, which usually means either a liquid-jet injector (wasteful of precious protein) or a "fixed-target" chip that traps crystals in a grid. Most fixed-target chips are made of silicon or PDMS, both of which scatter X-rays and are impractical to mass-produce, and neither plays well with the robots that synchrotrons now use to load samples automatically.

I designed an array-format fixed-target device (AFD-X) out of a low-scatter, highly optically transparent polymer, sized and shaped to drop directly into the robotic sample-changers already installed at synchrotron beamlines — specifically the Stanford Automated Mounter at SSRL — so an entire experiment can run as fully remote, automated data collection under controlled humidity, with no one standing at the beamline. I built two manufacturing routes for the chip itself: a benchtop photolithography process for small batches, and a continuous roll-to-roll UV nanoimprinting process that prints the devices onto a moving polymer web, which is what makes the design viable at real scale and low cost. I validated the device against three structurally very different proteins — lysozyme, thaumatin, and proteinase K — each solved from room-temperature data collected remotely.

LEAP-X : LEGO-style microfluidics you snap together

Lab on a Chip · 2026 · First author

(No figure shown here — this entry is summarized from the published record rather than the manuscript PDF.)

Every new crystallization condition or channel geometry usually means designing and fabricating an entirely new chip from scratch — slow, and wasteful when you're screening many conditions in parallel. This project builds the chip out of small, modular, interlocking pieces, LEGO-brick style, so channel networks and valve arrangements can be assembled and rearranged by hand between experiments instead of redesigned in CAD each time.

In place of the pumps or centrifugal spinning used in earlier designs, valves here are electrically actuated, opening on a small applied voltage for precise, on-demand digital control over exactly when protein and precipitant streams are allowed to mix. Crystals grown in the assembled device are analyzed by in situ X-ray crystallography without leaving the chip, and I mentored two undergraduate researchers through the build and validation of this platform.

HoTDoG : graphene microfluidics to visualize proteins at high temperature

bioRxiv 2026 · submitted to Science · Co-first author

Roughly 90% of protein structures in the Protein Data Bank were solved at cryogenic temperature (around −173 °C), mainly because frozen crystals are so much easier to handle — but proteins don't function at −173 °C. A structure collected that cold can systematically miss the exact conformational motions that make an enzyme fast, which is a real problem if the goal is to understand catalysis rather than just draw a static picture of a molecule.

With collaborators at the Kern Lab (Scripps/HHMI), I helped build a device that sandwiches a protein crystal between two sheets of graphene — a material one atom thick, strong enough to withstand handling, transparent to both visible light and X-rays, and an outstanding barrier to water vapor — so the crystal stays bathed in its own mother liquor while a temperature-controlled nitrogen stream holds it anywhere from cryogenic up past 65 °C, monitored live with an infrared camera. We used the device to collect high-resolution structures of three homologs of the enzyme orotidine 5′-monophosphate decarboxylase — from a cold-loving, a human, and a heat-loving organism — across that temperature range, and could directly watch each enzyme's active-site ensemble shift toward a catalytically "reactive" geometry exactly where its measured reaction rate says it should, a picture no single cryogenic snapshot could ever show.
